transcript: Okay, so how do I decide what to work on first when everything feels urgent. Um, that's a big question for marketing because honestly it feels like everything is always urgent. Let me, let me start from the beginning, because the context matters. At my last company I was the only marketing coordinator, so I supported the marketing manager but I also got requests from sales, from the founders, sometimes from customer success, and even from HR when they wanted recruiting posts. So on a normal Monday I might have, like, a sales deck to update, three social posts, a webinar to set up, the newsletter, and someone asking for a banner for an event that was, you know, tomorrow. And all of them would say it's urgent. So what I did at first, I'll be honest, was I just did whatever came in first, or whoever messaged me the most. That didn't work very well, because the loud requests aren't always the important ones. My manager noticed I was always busy but the campaign work, the stuff that actually brought leads, was always late. So we sat down and she helped me set up a board, like a Trello board, with columns for requests, this week, doing and done. And we agreed that campaign work, anything connected to the quarterly lead target, goes first. Then sales support, because it's close to revenue. Then everything else. I also started asking people when they really needed something, not just if it was urgent. Because a lot of the time when you ask, okay, when exactly do you need it, they say, oh, end of the week is fine. Which is very different from urgent. Um, another thing I did, I blocked Tuesday and Thursday mornings for deep work, like writing and campaign setup, and I didn't answer messages then unless it was really an emergency. At first people were a bit annoyed but after a few weeks they got used to it. It made me a lot more productive, I'm sure of that. There were still hard weeks. I remember one week before a big trade show, the founders wanted new brochures, sales wanted a new deck, and we also had a product launch email going out. I couldn't do everything, so I went to my manager with the list and asked her to choose. She moved the deck to the week after. That was the first time I really understood that it's okay to say something will wait, as long as you tell people early and it's agreed with your manager. Tools help too, but only if everyone uses them. For a while sales kept messaging me directly instead of putting requests on the board, so I'd copy their messages onto the board myself so at least I could see everything in one place. Eventually the sales lead told her team to use the board, which helped a lot. So to summarise, my approach is, first I try to understand what's connected to the company's goals, like leads or revenue. Then I ask when things are really needed. Then I plan my week with some protected time, and if there's too much, I go to my manager and we decide together what waits. And I try to tell people when they'll get their thing so they don't have to keep asking me. I'm still improving at it, especially saying no, or not yet, to senior people, that's still hard for me. But I'm much better than when I started. Sorry, that was a long answer, I just wanted to give you the full picture of how I work.
